effort: All-out: no cap needed. Nothing the lab checks in this test can do harm here (nearest people and buildings 5 m away), so they go all-out.Courtesy ceiling: none. Nothing in this test does harm, even all-out, with the nearest people and buildings 5 m away.
happens: Newton’s third law: the push between their hands is the same both ways. Each one’s own push back goes to his source (They take their own recoil), but the other’s press on him is real (a contest lets force move). Under the rules each grips the table’s peg with his free hand and rests his elbow on a pad bolted to the table, so each pad holds the other’s press, and the table carries the push between them, not their feet. Held together by their power (Things keep their form), the table never breaks, so arm strength decides.In people, a full-force twist like this is how the upper arm snaps: in one series of 30 arm-wrestling fractures, all were spiral breaks of the humerus. A healthy humerus takes roughly 190 N·m in theory; cadaver bones broke at 25–31 N·m. Rex and Ollie are indestructible.
math: Arm force = 25% of strength in both muscle models (estimate, plausibly 10–40%: ordinary men’s measured arm force against an assumed 1–2× body-weight deadlift): Rex 222 kN, Ollie 222 kN. The table carries the push while both arms stay under any limit (Things keep their form: they hold it) (each pad holds the other’s press). Once it breaks they stand: each presses with his full arm force (his push back goes to his source, so his footing doesn’t cap it), and each one’s feet hold against the other’s press: footing = μ × min(m g, what the ground under his feet bears); unlimited if bolted. The stronger press pins the weaker arm. Twist on each upper arm = the force his own arm presses with × 0.19 × his height. A pinned arm still presses with all it has; an arm that holds carries the whole push. Gravity between them: F = G m₁ m₂ / d², d = 1.91 m across the table.

arm-keepoff.verdict: The table breaks first: both arms out-push its 15.1 kN. Arm-wrestling standing up, it’s a dead heat at 222 kN: their arms are locked. But each one’s press beats the other’s footing (17.7 kN), so both are pushed off their feet, opposite ways, turning about their clasped hands. The lab doesn’t follow that motion.

happens: Newton’s third law: Ollie pushes Rex exactly as hard as Rex pushes back. Ollie takes his own recoil, so his side of that push goes to his source, not through his feet into the ground: his footing doesn’t cap his push. Rex’s side goes through his feet into the ground, so he holds only as much as his footing takes. (This is a contest, so the push on Rex is real.)Footing here: Ollie’s push doesn’t depend on his feet; Rex holds 17.7 kN (his footing).For a walk-out or a shove-off, see Wrestle.
